q: Light is a form of energy which stimulates our sense of vision.
e: True. Light is a form of energy which stimulates our sense of vision. Lenses refract. Light is an electromagnetic wave and also a particle.

q: By the middle of the seventeenth century, two theories about the nature of light were introduced: corpuscular theory and wave theory of light.
e: True. By the middle of the seventeenth century, two theories about the nature of light were introduced: corpuscular theory and wave theory of light. By the mid-1600s there were two pictures of light: Newton's particles and Huygens' waves.

q: Newton suggested that light was made up of a stream of tiny waves known as corpuscles.
e: False. Newton called his light particles corpuscles, not photons. Photon is the later quantum name.

q: Newton's corpuscular theory could explain the phenomena of reflection and refraction of light.
e: True. Newton's corpuscular theory could explain the phenomena of reflection and refraction of light. Refraction: light bends when the speed changes across a boundary. Snell's law is n1 sin i = n2 sin r.

q: Huygens, contemporary of Newton, suggested that like water waves and sound waves, light also has wave nature.
e: True. Huygens, contemporary of Newton, suggested that like water waves and sound waves, light also has wave nature. Huygens treated light as a wave. Each point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets.

q: The majority of scientists accepted the wave theory of light immediately.
e: False. The wave theory explains interference, diffraction, and polarisation.

q: Light, in fact, cannot bend round an obstacle.
e: False. Lenses refract. Light is an electromagnetic wave and also a particle. The written line says Light, in fact, cannot bend round an obstacle.

q: The wavelengths of light are so short compared to those of water waves and sound waves that the bending of light cannot be ordinarily observed.
e: True. The wavelengths of light are so short compared to those of water waves and sound waves that the bending of light cannot be ordinarily observed. Light does diffract, but its wavelength is tiny, so the bend is hard to see.

q: It was discovered by the end of the nineteenth century that light consists of electromagnetic waves.
e: True. It was discovered by the end of the nineteenth century that light consists of electromagnetic waves. By the late 1800s light was known to be an electromagnetic wave.

q: It was found at the beginning of the twentieth century that in addition to the wave nature, light has corpuscular or particle nature as well.
e: True. It was found at the beginning of the twentieth century that in addition to the wave nature, light has corpuscular or particle nature as well. Lenses refract. Light is an electromagnetic wave and also a particle.

q: Today, it is generally accepted that light has only wave nature.
e: False. Light has wave-particle duality: electromagnetic waves and photons together, not one picture alone.

q: The corpuscular theory and wave theory of light are not contradictory but are complementary to each other.
e: True. The corpuscular theory and wave theory of light are not contradictory but are complementary to each other. The wave theory explains interference, diffraction, and polarisation.
